hero.eyebrow: Case study · The real cost of a manual process
hero.title: Close to $56,000 a year, hidden in a task that nobody had ever put a number on.
hero.lead: Every week, a team retyped its suppliers’ prices by hand into its point-of-sale (POS) system. It looked like a small chore. Added up over the year, it was the equivalent of a part-time salary — spent retyping numbers. We built the system that does it for them. And because it compares every supplier on every order, the business now buys at the best price: margin regained, on top of the time.

money.sub: The equivalent of a part-time position, given back to the team for work that actually grows the business.
money.plus: + the margin regained on every product bought at the best price.

problem.title: The task wasn’t on the books. It was on the payroll.
problem.p1: Nobody had ever added up the hours. Updating prices was accepted as a normal chore, a necessary evil of the trade. But every supplier list — tens of thousands of lines — was retyped by hand, week after week.
problem.p2: Put end to end, this invisible work cost close to $56,000 a year in time. Not counting data-entry errors, and not counting the money left on the table every time a product was ordered from the most expensive supplier because there was no way to compare.

items.title: We put a number on the invisible
items.text: The first step was putting a dollar figure on the chore. Once the loss became a number, the decision made itself.

items.title: The machine copies, not the team
items.text: The system imports every supplier’s list, compares prices product by product and prepares the update. All the team has to do is approve — on one screen, not over three days.

items.title: Plugged into the existing POS
items.text: Everything connects to the point-of-sale system already in place, without replacing it and without interrupting operations. The switchover happened without the store closing for a single day.

note.eyebrow: This isn’t a grocery store story
note.quote: Every SMB has a $56,000 task. Almost nobody has put a number on it.
note.body: A weekly chore everyone accepts because “that’s how we’ve always done it.” It shows up nowhere in the financial statements, but it’s there every week, on someone’s payroll. Finding it and putting a number on it is already half the work.
